prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Constellation Energy Corp" (ticker CEG), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "CEG", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Constellation Energy Corporation
result.industry: Independent power producer and energy retailer (nuclear-led)
markets: Wholesale electricity generation (PJM, Midwest, New York, ERCOT, California)
Long-term clean power contracts with data centers and large companies
Retail electricity and natural gas supply to businesses and homes
Capacity and clean-energy attribute markets (ZECs, RECs)

mission.statement: At Constellation, we are accelerating the transition to a carbon-free future.
mission.source: Company website, 'What We Stand For' page (constellationenergy.com/our-company/what-we-stand-for.html)
mission.plain: Constellation wants America to get more of its electricity from power plants that don't pollute the air with carbon.

about.plain: Constellation owns the biggest group of nuclear power plants in America, plus gas, geothermal, water and wind plants. These plants make electricity all day and night. It sells that electricity to the grid and directly to companies, cities and families. Big tech companies now sign 20-year deals with it to power their data centers.
about.customers: Grid operators and utilities, about three-quarters of the Fortune 100, tech giants like Microsoft, Meta and Google, and about 2.5 million business and household accounts.
about.everyday: When a home or office in Illinois, Pennsylvania or Texas turns on the lights, there is a good chance part of that power came from a Constellation plant.

money.plain: carbon-free electricity from about 22 GW of reactors sold to the grid

money.part: Selling power and gas to businesses and homes
money.plain: electricity and gas supply contracts for companies and households

money.part: Gas and geothermal plants from Calpine
money.plain: about 23 GW of gas, geothermal (The Geysers) and battery plants bought in January 2026
20-year power contracts with Microsoft (Crane restart), Meta (Clinton) and Google (890 MW of uprates)

money.part: New nuclear: restarts, uprates and small reactors
money.plain: restarting Crane (Three Mile Island Unit 1) in 2027, adding output at existing reactors, studying small modular reactors

result.summary: Constellation has a real and hard-to-copy advantage: it owns about 22 GW across 25 US reactors, the largest nuclear fleet in the country, at a time when new nuclear plants take over a decade to build and data centers want around-the-clock carbon-free power. Its retail arm is the largest US supplier of commercial and industrial power by volume. But it still sells much of its output into commodity power markets, so its profits swing with power and gas prices and with government policy.

pricingPower.evidence: Scarce carbon-free baseload lets it sign 20-year premium PPAs (Microsoft for the 835 MW Crane restart, Sept 2024; Meta for Clinton's 1,121 MW, June 2025; Google for 890 MW of uprates plus 2,700 MW supply, Oct 2026), but merchant output is a price-taker: FY2025 operating income fell to $3,086M from $4,352M in FY2024 as purchased power and fuel costs rose to $14,681M from $11,419M.

moats.evidence: The Constellation name matters to corporate buyers seeking clean power, but electricity is a commodity and few consumers choose suppliers by brand.
Hyperscaler PPAs run 15-20 years and are tied to specific plants, while C&I retail customers renew at 77% (power) and 84% (gas) on roughly two-year contracts, per the FY2025 10-K.
One more customer does not make the power more valuable to other customers.

With about 55 GW after Calpine and a 25-unit nuclear fleet running at 93-95% capacity factors, it spreads fuel buying, outage crews and licensing costs over the largest private-sector fleet, and reports the nation's largest C&I and residential power supply volumes.
Power markets in PJM and ERCOT are open to rivals, but transmission constraints, interconnection queues and plant siting limit how much new competing supply can arrive in a given region.
Rivals such as Vistra and Talen also own nuclear plants and can copy its data-center contracting model.

Decades of nuclear operating experience (fleet capacity factor 93.0% in Q2 2026, excluding Salem and STP) and the ability to restart a retired reactor (Crane) and license 20-year extensions are skills few operators have.

It owns roughly 22 GW of existing licensed US nuclear capacity, about a fifth of the US fleet, and new reactors cost tens of billions and take 10+ years, so this carbon-free baseload cannot easily be replicated.

customers.evidence: C&I renewal rates were 77% for power and 84% for gas in 2025 with an average customer life of about six years, and it serves three-quarters of the Fortune 100, but there is little public NPS data and residential customers mainly shop on price.

talent.evidence: Certified as a Great Place to Work for the fourth straight year (2026) and named to The Civic 50; it employs one of the largest nuclear workforces in the US, though it does not feature in top employer rankings such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

product.evidence: Its nuclear fleet runs at about 93-95% capacity factors and delivers 24/7 carbon-free power that wind and solar cannot match, which is why Microsoft, Meta and Google chose it for long-term clean-energy deals; the 2025 ERM benchmark ranked its fleet the cleanest large generation portfolio in the US.

competitors.name: Vistra Corp.
competitors.note: Texas-based generator and retailer with nuclear (Comanche Peak, Energy Harbor plants), gas and coal; competes for hyperscaler deals, ERCOT and PJM power and retail customers.

competitors.name: NRG Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Large retail electricity and gas supplier (Reliant, Direct Energy) and gas generator in ERCOT and PJM.

competitors.name: Talen Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Owns Susquehanna nuclear plant in PJM and signed a data-center supply deal with Amazon.

competitors.name: Public Service Enterprise Group (PSEG Power)
competitors.note: Co-owns the Salem and Hope Creek nuclear plants in New Jersey and sells power into PJM.

competitors.name: NextEra Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Largest US renewable developer; supplies long-term clean power to corporates and plans the Duane Arnold nuclear restart.

competitors.name: Dominion Energy, Inc.
competitors.note: Regulated utility serving Virginia's data-center hub and owner of nuclear plants; competes for SMR and data-center supply.

competitors.name: Duke Energy Corporation
competitors.note: Regulated utility and large nuclear operator in the Carolinas competing to serve data centers in its territory.

competitors.name: The Southern Company
competitors.note: Regulated utility with Vogtle nuclear units, serving large new loads in Georgia.

competitors.name: Brookfield Renewable Partners
competitors.note: Hydro, wind and solar supplier with large framework deals with Microsoft and Google.

competitors.name: ENGIE SA
competitors.note: Competes in US C&I retail power supply and corporate renewable PPAs.

competitors.name: LS Power
competitors.note: Private owner of gas plants in PJM and ERCOT; buying assets Constellation divests for the Calpine deal.

competitors.name: Oklo Inc.
competitors.note: Developer of small advanced reactors that hopes to sell power directly to data centers in the 2030s.

marketShare.market: US commercial and industrial direct retail power supply
marketShare.measure: share of C&I direct customer business

threats: Lower wholesale power and capacity prices (or PJM capacity price caps) would cut merchant earnings, as in FY2025 when operating income fell 29%.
Political and regulatory pushback on behind-the-meter data-center deals and on rising consumer power bills in PJM.
Weaker-than-expected AI data-center demand or hyperscalers building their own generation (SMRs, gas) instead of buying from incumbents.
Rivals (Vistra, Talen, NextEra) competing for the same hyperscaler contracts and nuclear uprates.
Nuclear operating risk: extended outages, safety events or delays to the Crane restart targeted for 2027.
Integration of the Calpine acquisition and higher leverage: total debt rose to $24.7B at June 30, 2026 from $9.0B at end-2025.
Loss or change of federal nuclear production tax credits and state support programs.

ceo.name: Joseph Dominguez
ceo.background: Mechanical engineer (NJIT) and lawyer (Rutgers Law, magna cum laude); former federal prosecutor, Exelon public-policy executive and ComEd CEO

c1.evidence: It is the clear leader in US nuclear power (about 22 GW, 25 units), and demand for 24/7 clean power for AI data centers is growing fast, but power generation itself is a mature, century-old industry.

c2.evidence: Hyperscalers choose it because only existing reactors can deliver large amounts of carbon-free 24/7 power soon, as shown by 20-year deals with Microsoft (Crane, 2024), Meta (Clinton, 2025) and Google (890 MW uprates, 2026), and that nuclear fleet would take decades to copy.

c3.evidence: It is the default leader in US nuclear power and the largest C&I power supplier, but ordinary people mostly know it only as a name on their power bill, if at all.

c4.evidence: It repeats its purpose of 'accelerating the transition to a carbon-free future' and is restarting a retired reactor, but it is a profit-driven merchant generator that just bought Calpine's large gas fleet.

c6.evidence: “nuclear, clean energy, AI power supplier” — the impression is mostly positive among investors and tech buyers, though some consumer advocates link it to rising power bills in PJM.

c7.evidence: US power demand is rising for the first time in decades because of data centers, electrification and reshoring, and it has signed multiple 15-20 year contracts, including 920 MW of new nuclear PPAs announced in Q2 2026.

c8.evidence: It can grow through uprates (Google deal), restarts (Crane), license extensions, the Calpine gas and geothermal fleet, and possibly small modular reactors, but it remains a US power company.

m1.evidence: Dominguez argued early that existing nuclear plants would be essential for AI and clean-energy goals and turned that view into the Microsoft, Meta and Google deals and the Calpine acquisition.

m2.evidence: He is not a founder but has led the company since its 2022 spin-off from Exelon with long-dated bets such as the Crane restart and 20-year license renewals.

m4.evidence: There is little public evidence either way about a servant-leadership style beyond Great Place to Work certification for four straight years.

m5.evidence: Its culture is built on nuclear operating discipline (93-95% capacity factors) rather than on inventing new products, though it is pursuing uprates, restarts and new reactor studies.

m6.evidence: Dominguez has a mechanical engineering degree but built his career as a lawyer, prosecutor and policy executive rather than as a plant engineer.

m7.evidence: No clear public evidence of a purpose beyond the company's carbon-free mission and community programs such as The Civic 50 recognition.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Joseph Dominguez at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: He is a well-known industry voice on nuclear and AI power but not a celebrity CEO with a distinctive public persona.

m9.evidence: Since the 2022 spin-off he has signed landmark hyperscaler deals, closed the Calpine acquisition in January 2026 and lifted 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $11.50-$12.50, while the stock rose several-fold from its 2022 listing.

m10.evidence: No public evidence of a notable frugality culture.

c10.evidence: Its electricity keeps homes, businesses and data centers running across much of the US, but it serves one country, not the whole world.

p2.evidence: Safely running 25 nuclear reactors and restarting a retired one is extremely hard, heavily regulated and important for reliable, carbon-free power.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose from $17,603M (FY2020) to $25,533M (FY2025) but fell in FY2024 to $23,568M from $24,918M because power prices dropped.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 1.5% in FY2020 ($256M on $17,603M) to 12.1% in FY2025 ($3,086M on $25,533M), though it peaked at 18.5% in FY2024.

f3.evidence: Shareholders' equity is positive at $31,977M (June 30, 2026), but debt of $24,700M far exceeds cash of $697M after the Calpine acquisition.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $256M in FY2020 to $3,086M in FY2025, but operating cash flow was negative in FY2023-FY2024 (-$5,301M, -$2,464M) because receivables collections were booked as investing cash (DPP), before reaching $4,237M in FY2025.

v1.evidence: For companies wanting large, round-the-clock carbon-free power now, its nuclear fleet is the best option, but for most buyers its electricity is the same as anyone else's.

v2.evidence: It has been Great Place to Work certified four years running (2026), but it does not appear on top lists such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: It produces about a fifth of America's carbon-free nuclear power; if it vanished, grid operators in PJM, Illinois and New York, its 2.5 million customer accounts and tech companies like Microsoft and Meta would face shortages and more fossil-fuel generation.
